ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Orthopaedic Surgery (foot and ankle) Consultation — Sitting Bull — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: One-week review, seen the same day by orthopaedic foot and ankle surgery: CT, the diagnosis, retained fragments and lead, and the treatment options

text.paragraph: Chronic pain of the left ankle and hindfoot with a limp in a man of about 55, decades after a gunshot wound to the foot, with arthritis and small metallic densities on X-ray. Please confirm the diagnosis, advise on the retained metal and on non-operative and surgical treatment, and help us keep his care close to home and in line with his wishes. [S]
Urgency: Routine; at the visiting foot and ankle session one week from now, on the same day as his one-week primary care visit. [S]

list.item: Is this post-traumatic arthritis, which joints are involved, and is there any sign of chronic infection from the old wound?
Should the retained metal fragments be removed, and is he at risk of lead toxicity?
Which non-operative treatments do you advise: brace, physical therapy, anti-inflammatory medicines, injection?
What would surgery involve, and when would it be reasonable?
How can his care be kept close to home and shaped by his own choices?

text.paragraph: Sitting Bull, a Hunkpapa Lakota leader of about 55, is seen with the clinic interpreter at the request of Dr. Talltree-Hastings. Many years ago he was shot in the foot in a fight; the wound healed, but he has limped since. Over the past two years the pain below the ankle has worsened, with morning stiffness, pain on uneven ground and difficulty riding. He wants to keep walking and riding, prefers to avoid surgery, and wants to understand every option before deciding. He asked to be called Sitting Bull. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Sitting Bull was born in the early 1830s, between 1831 and 1837 by the reckoning of different sources, into a prominent Hunkpapa Lakota family near the Grand River in present-day South Dakota, at a place called Many Caches. [D]

His boyhood name was Jumping Badger, and he was called Slow for his deliberate ways; as a young man he received his father's name, Tȟatȟáŋka Íyotake (Sitting Bull), also written Tatanka Iyotake or Tatanka-Iyotanka. [D]

He became a leading Hunkpapa warrior, hunter and leader, admitted to respected warrior societies, and by about 1866 or 1867 was recognized as an important political and military leader of the Lakota bands resisting encroachment on their lands. [D]

He was also a holy man, a wichasha wakan (in the modern Lakota orthography wičháša wakȟáŋ), whose calling was confirmed in the Sun Dance; historians note that equating a wichasha wakan with a medicine man is misleading. [D]

In a fight with Crow warriors, about 1856 by his biographer's account, he was shot in the foot: the Crow chief's shot struck his shield and then cut a groove along his foot from heel to toe. The wound troubled him for the rest of his life and left him with a limp. [D]
In 1864 he was again wounded, through the hip and back, in an attack on a wagon train crossing Lakota territory. [D]

In June 1876, before the battle at the Little Bighorn (the Greasy Grass), he led a Sun Dance on Rosebud Creek, offering fifty pieces of flesh from each arm and fasting, and had a vision of soldiers falling into the camp; his village was attacked later that month, and he, beyond fighting age, did not fight himself. [D]
After the battle the army pursued the Lakota bands, and in 1877 he led his people north into Canada, where the buffalo were scarce, food was short, sickness spread and the winters were hard. [D]

Starving, he and the remaining Hunkpapa surrendered at Fort Buford, Dakota Territory, on July 20, 1881; despite promises that they would go to Standing Rock, he and his followers were held as prisoners of war at Fort Randall for nearly two years. [D]

In May 1883 he was allowed to join his people at the Standing Rock Reservation, where there were too few bison to support the Hunkpapa, he was sent to work in the farm fields, and he chose to live in a cabin on the Grand River near where he was born. [D]
He toured with Wild West shows in 1884 and 1885, spending four months of 1885 with William F. Cody's show, and then returned to Standing Rock, where the agent would not let him rejoin the show. [D]

list.item: Post-traumatic osteoarthritis of the left subtalar and talonavicular joints (M19.172). The pattern on X-ray and CT, with the old wound track through the heel, is post-traumatic arthritis of the posterior subtalar and talonavicular joints; the ankle joint itself is spared. A healed, non-draining scar, normal inflammatory markers and no bone changes of infection on CT make chronic osteomyelitis very unlikely. [S]

Retained metal fragments (Z18.12). Lead from retained bullet fragments is absorbed mainly when fragments sit in a joint, bone or other fluid-filled space; his lie in soft tissue, and his blood lead is low. Removal would mean surgery through scarred heel skin for no benefit, so they should stay. [S]

Non-operative treatment (M19.172). The ACR/Arthritis Foundation guideline covers the hand, hip and knee, but its core advice applies here: exercise and therapy, an orthosis that limits painful motion, topical then oral NSAIDs for limited periods, and intra-articular corticosteroid injection. A rigid ankle-foot orthosis and a rocker-sole shoe reduce subtalar motion. A short course of naproxen is reasonable with normal kidney function and blood pressure, watching his stomach. An ultrasound-guided subtalar injection is both a test and a treatment. Opioids have no place here. [S]

Surgery (M19.172). If pain stops him walking or riding despite these measures, a subtalar arthrodesis, or a double arthrodesis that includes the talonavicular joint, reliably relieves pain but removes side-to-side motion of the hindfoot, needs about three months without weight on the foot and a year to recover fully, and would change how he rides. It is his decision, and there is no harm in waiting. [S]

Care close to home. He lives an hour from the clinic. Therapy by video, rides through the Community Health Representative program and visits at the outreach session keep his care close to home; the interpreter at each visit and his own choices, including traditional healing if he wishes, should shape the plan. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Talltree-Hastings's intake note. Weight-bearing X-rays of the left foot and ankle from intake. CT of the left foot this morning: post-traumatic arthritis of the posterior subtalar and talonavicular joints with subchondral cysts; ankle joint preserved; four small metal fragments, the largest 3 mm, in the plantar soft tissue of the heel, none in a joint or bone; no sign of bone infection. Blood count, creatinine, C-reactive protein and sedimentation rate normal; hemoglobin A1c 6.0%. Home blood pressure average 124/78 mmHg. Point-of-care blood lead today 2.4 ug/dL. [S]

list.item: A rigid ankle-foot orthosis molded by the orthotist, with a rocker-sole shoe. [S]
Physical therapy weekly for six weeks with a home program for hindfoot mobility, strength and balance. [S]
Continue diclofenac gel; naproxen 500 mg twice daily with food for up to six weeks; stop for stomach pain or black stools. [S]
If pain stays above 4 of 10 after four to six weeks, an ultrasound-guided subtalar corticosteroid injection, no more than three or four a year. [S]
Leave the metal fragments in place; repeat blood lead only for symptoms of lead toxicity or if a fragment moves into a joint. [S]
No opioids. [S]
Arthrodesis only if he chooses it after the non-operative plan; I will see him again at any outreach session if he wishes to discuss it. [S]
If travel to therapy becomes hard, video sessions and rides through the Community Health Representative program. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Talltree-Hastings, who saw him the same day. The findings and every option were explained through the interpreter; he chose the brace, therapy, naproxen and, if needed, the injection, and asked for time before thinking about surgery. [S]

Follow-up: Dr. Talltree-Hastings continues his care and will give the subtalar injection at the clinic; orthopaedics will see him at the outreach session if non-operative care fails or he wants to discuss surgery. [S]
